deckTitle: Grimms' Kayfabe Legends — Expansion Set 02: The Fairy Tale Screwjob

cards.power: The Sticky Gimmick. Opponent cannot tag out. If they grapple, they get stuck to you.
cards.lore: He who holds the goose holds the heat. Everyone else is just a hanger-on.
cards.gradeReason: "Cannot tag out" is wrestling idiom without a Kayfabizarro translation — the sticky concept is right but the table needs to invent what it means.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: wrestling trading card. Subject: golden goose with a crowd of humans and animals stuck to its feathers, mid-waddle. Mood: involuntary solidarity.

cards.power: Diminishing Returns. Trade this card for a "Horse," then a "Cow," then a "Pig," until you have nothing but a stone.
cards.lore: I have this load to carry... it hurts my shoulder sadly.
cards.gradeReason: Sequential self-degradation down to a stone is the Hans in Luck story enacted as a mechanical suicide run — the table watches you dismantle yourself.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: engraving. Subject: stone with a tragic face half-buried, a discarded saddle and horseshoe nearby. Mood: cheerful ruin.

cards.power: Botched Spot. Roll a d6. On a 1, you burst with laughter and your belly seam splits. Skip a turn.
cards.lore: The coal, who was of an impetuous disposition, tripped quite boldly... and breathed her last.
cards.gradeReason: Risk of catastrophic laughter-failure on a 1 is a brilliantly self-aware wrestling botch — the table will try to trigger it.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: punk wrestling poster. Subject: straw, coal, and bean performing a spot that is clearly going wrong, seams visible. Mood: impending disaster.

cards.power: The Push. Gain immense stats for one turn. Afterwards, your envious brother tries to hang you.
cards.lore: Compared to this vegetable, all the learning of the schools is as empty air.
cards.gradeReason: The aftermath trigger is the best part, but "your envious brother tries to hang you" has no mechanical definition — the table invents the consequence.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: dark woodcut. Subject: enormous turnip with a suspicious sibling visible in the background with rope. Mood: peak followed immediately by consequence.

cards.power: Top Rope Finisher. Instantly defeat a "Stepmother" type enemy. You die in the process.
cards.lore: Crash! The bird threw the millstone down on her head, and she was crushed to death.
cards.gradeReason: Kamikaze finisher with type-specific targeting is the most self-sacrificing move in the deck — you win by dying, which is correct.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: brutal woodcut. Subject: millstone dropping from great height, a figure in formal dress below not having looked up yet. Mood: terminal velocity.

cards.power: Kayfabe Strength. Bluff any Strength check. If called out, you must squeeze water from a stone (actually cheese).
cards.lore: The giant read: "Seven at one stroke," and began to feel a little respect for the tiny fellow.
cards.gradeReason: The "(actually cheese)" parenthetical is the best four-word reveal in the deck — the bluff only works until someone demands the proof.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: wrestling championship belt design. Subject: ornate belt buckle reading "7 AT ONE BLOW," circled by seven bewildered flies. Mood: manufactured prestige.

cards.power: The Sleeper Hold. Opponent falls unconscious until the lace is cut or comb removed.
cards.lore: She set to work so nimbly... that Snowdrop's breath was stopped, and she fell down as if she were dead.
cards.gradeReason: "Until the lace is cut or comb removed" requires physical objects not present at a card table — the removal condition is theatrically stranded.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: gothic engraving. Subject: poisoned comb dripping green, baroque mirror behind, no one in the frame. Mood: crime after the fact.

cards.power: The Beard Trap. Trap an opponent's facial hair. They yield their gold or lose the beard.
cards.lore: I can do better than that... and in it caught the old man's beard. Crime scene!
cards.gradeReason: "Yield gold or lose the beard" is an outstanding two-option squeeze — either outcome is humiliating and the table will not forget who played this.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: crime scene woodcut. Subject: enormous beard caught in an anvil, owner in shock, gold coins visible nearby. Mood: follicular hostage.

cards.power: The Stable Entrance. Break through any window. Terrify robbers. Eat their food.
cards.lore: The ass brayed, the dog barked, the cat mewed, and the cock screamed.
cards.gradeReason: Three sequential actions in a single power — break, terrify, eat — is chaos with cause and effect, precisely as chaotic as the source tale.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: wrestling entrance poster. Subject: donkey, dog, cat, rooster stacked in fighting poses, mid-entrance. Mood: accidental terror.

cards.power: Squash Match Reversal. If eaten, you may cut your way out of the opponent's belly. Fill with stones.
cards.lore: We will not open the door; you are the wolf!
cards.gradeReason: "If eaten" trigger is brilliantly conditional but requires "eaten" to be a defined game state — without faction rules it floats as a concept.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: dark children's book engraving. Subject: seven small goats emerging from a wolf's stomach, each carrying a stone. Mood: improbable reversal.

cards.power: Crowd Support. Recover lost items from the discard pile.
cards.lore: We will remember you—one good turn deserves another!
cards.gradeReason: "Crowd Support" is a generic discard-retrieval mechanic with a lore that states the moral — it describes the reward instead of activating it.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: protest woodcut. Subject: ants and ducks marching with FAIR WAGES signs, recovering dropped items in formation. Mood: organized mutual aid.

cards.power: Stamina Drain. Force opponent to dance all night. Their footwear is destroyed.
cards.lore: Every morning their shoes were found to be quite worn through as if they had been danced in all night.
cards.gradeReason: Forcing an opponent to dance until their footwear is mechanically destroyed is both punishment and performance — the table has to decide how the dancing manifests.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: dark ballroom engraving. Subject: twelve pairs of shredded shoes in a pile, a scoreboard counting the hours. Mood: mandatory exhaustion.

cards.power: The Promo. Reveal the highest stat card in the deck. Enrage the current Queen.
cards.lore: Thou, queen, art the fairest in all this land: But Snowdrop... is lovelier far than thee.
cards.gradeReason: The promo-as-information-attack is sharp but "Enrage the current Queen" requires a designated Queen player — a setup assumption the table must pre-agree.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: gothic portrait. Subject: ornate frame containing a grinning sportscaster face delivering bad news. Mood: unsolicited truth.

cards.power: Face Turn. Disguise your "Rough Voice." You count as a "Mother" type for one turn.
cards.lore: The wolf went to a shopkeeper and bought himself a great lump of chalk... and made his voice soft.
cards.gradeReason: Faction-flipping via voice disguise is conceptually perfect but requires a "Mother" type category that needs table definition.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: woodcut police lineup. Subject: wolf swallowing chalk, throat visibly softening, wearing glasses. Mood: unconvincing transformation.

cards.power: Post-Mortem Commentary. Reveal hidden truths about the "False Bride."
cards.lore: Alas! alas! if thy mother knew it, Sadly, sadly, would she rue it.
cards.gradeReason: "Reveal hidden truths" has no mechanical specification — what gets revealed, by whom, and to what effect is entirely undefined.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: horror engraving. Subject: severed horse head mounted above a gate, speaking calmly to passersby. Mood: posthumous testimony.

cards.power: The Catchphrase. Sing a song so repetitive it causes madness or death.
cards.lore: Kywitt, Kywitt, what a beautiful bird am I!
cards.gradeReason: Requiring a player to actually sing something repetitive until it causes madness is the most physically committed card in the deck.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: glam-metal record sleeve. Subject: small bird at a microphone with a gold chain, eyes rolling back, audience reacting with hands over ears. Mood: compulsory encore.

cards.power: Budget Cuts. Exile two 'Child' cards to save food resources.
cards.lore: "You fool! Then we must all four die of hunger."
cards.gradeReason: Abandonment as fiscal policy — the power names the cruelty and gives it an economic rationale that is both accurate and devastating.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: corporate horror engraving. Subject: stepmother in boardroom chair, two small files labeled CHILD 1 and CHILD 2 stamped EXILED. Mood: managerial necessity.

cards.power: Identity Theft. Swap hands with another player. Kill their horse to hide the evidence.
cards.lore: "I shall ride upon Falada, and you may have my horse instead."
cards.gradeReason: "Kill their horse to hide the evidence" transforms a standard hand-swap into a cover-up — the second sentence is what makes the first sentence criminal.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: true crime woodcut. Subject: woman in crown standing next to a horse that clearly knows something. Mood: preemptive silencing.

cards.power: The Contract. Spin "Straw" into "Gold." If opponent guesses your name, you self-destruct.
cards.lore: "The devil told you that! The devil told you that!"
cards.gradeReason: Self-destruct on correct naming is the most faithful Rumpelstiltskin mechanic possible — the card's own continued existence depends on staying anonymous.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: legal document horror. Subject: small furious figure tearing itself apart, spinning wheel in background, a correctly filled-in form on the floor. Mood: contractual catastrophe.

cards.power: Re-Booking. Replace the "Dead Husband" card with a "New Suitor" (Wolf, Dog, or Fox).
cards.lore: "Up with the window, fling out my old man!"
cards.gradeReason: Narrative re-casting as a game mechanic — replacing a dead entity with a new one from a defined species roster — is the most wrestling-booking move in the deck.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: talent agency document. Subject: cat reviewing headshots of wolf, dog, and fox for an urgent vacancy. Mood: pragmatic replacement.

cards.power: The Botched Transfer. If you try to move this to a "Golden Cage," you trigger the alarm.
cards.lore: "One feather is of no use to me, I must have the whole bird."
cards.gradeReason: Trap-object mechanic is clever — the prize is also a hazard — but "Golden Cage" requires a named card type not guaranteed to be in play.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: heist blueprint. Subject: golden bird in a cage surrounded by triggered alarm wires, thief mid-reach. Mood: successful failure.

cards.power: The Revive. Heal a "King" card. Beware of switching fluids.
cards.lore: "They waited till he was fast asleep... and took it for themselves, giving him bitter sea-water instead."
cards.gradeReason: "Beware of switching fluids" is an editorial comment, not a mechanic — the power description ends where the actual card interaction should begin.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: apothecary woodcut. Subject: two identical flagons side by side, one glowing gold, one with a skull label, hands reaching for the wrong one. Mood: fraternal sabotage.

cards.power: Fast Travel. Teleport to any "Mountain" or "Castle."
cards.lore: "Shoot into the midst of them... the cloak will fall too."
cards.gradeReason: Teleporting to named locations requires a board-state geography system that Kayfabizarro does not have — the power assumes a map that doesn't exist at the table.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: dark cloak illustration. Subject: cloak landing in a mountain pass, wearer already gone, birds scattering. Mood: fast and inexplicable departure.

cards.power: Infinite Resources. But only if you say the catchphrase "Bricklebrit!"
cards.lore: "Gold is good, but a stick that beats people by itself is better."
cards.gradeReason: Resources conditional on shouting "Bricklebrit!" turns mechanical advantage into public performance — no one at the table will say it quietly.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: tavern woodcut. Subject: self-setting table, gold-producing donkey, and flying stick, all triggered by one small person shouting upward. Mood: activated abundance.

cards.power: The Fattening. Detain an opponent. Check their finger for fatness every turn.
cards.lore: "Scream as he might, it would not help him."
cards.gradeReason: Finger-checking each turn is physical theatre that escalates in absurdity — the table will eventually refuse to extend a finger and create a rule crisis.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: surveillance horror. Subject: wooden cage with a finger-hole, hand extended through it, assessor checking with a measuring tape. Mood: clinical detention.

cards.power: The Table Turn. Reverse a "Grapple" move. The aggressor is incinerated.
cards.lore: "Push her in... and then shut the iron door and bolt it."
cards.gradeReason: Reversal with incineration consequence is mechanically clean but requires "Grapple" to be a defined move type — which it isn't in the core rules.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: medieval woodcut. Subject: oven door slamming shut with the wrong figure inside, child standing clear. Mood: corrective justice.

cards.power: Slippery Slope. No one can attack you, but you cannot move unless you have 'The Horse' or sacrifice a "Finger."
cards.lore: "Every time he attempted to climb he fell back again."
cards.gradeReason: Sanctuary with a specific painful exit condition is inventive, but both "The Horse" card and a sacrificed "Finger" are faction/token-dependent without base-game support.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: slick alpine engraving. Subject: perfectly smooth glass peak, figure repeatedly arriving at base with bloody hands. Mood: recursive failure.

cards.power: The Final Bump. The ultimate punishment for a "False Bride."
cards.lore: "Dragged along by two white horses from street to street till she is dead."
cards.gradeReason: "The ultimate punishment" is a description, not a mechanic — no die result, no card action, no table instruction exists beneath the power name.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: brutal woodcut. Subject: barrel studded with nails rolling downhill, two white horses departing in the distance. Mood: final adjudication.

cards.power: Accidental Genius. Guess an opponent's hand correctly by sheer luck or intimidation.
cards.lore: "That man knows everything!"
cards.gradeReason: The explicit permission to guess by intimidation rather than knowledge is the card's genius — it licenses bluster as a valid epistemology.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: village square woodcut. Subject: confused peasant with a diploma pointing at a rooster who is definitely guilty. Mood: accidental accuracy.

cards.power: Paralysis by Analysis. All players must stop and weep over a hypothetical future disaster.
cards.lore: "If the pick-axe should fall on his head... have we not reason to weep?"
cards.gradeReason: Mass forced weeping over a hypothetical is the most spectacular social theatre in the deck — someone at every table will refuse, which creates a second crisis.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: domestic tragedy engraving. Subject: entire party of people weeping around a barrel, pick-axe visible on a wall that is definitely stable. Mood: preemptive grief.

cards.power: Barking Mad. Understand the 'Dog' faction. Retrieve the treasure from the 'Haunted Tower.'
cards.lore: "I have learnt what the dogs say when they bark."
cards.gradeReason: Dog-faction literacy plus location retrieval is fun but chains together two undefined systems — Dog faction and Haunted Tower — requiring complete table invention.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: countryside illustration. Subject: small boy conferring seriously with a dog, both looking at a distant tower. Mood: unlikely alliance.

cards.power: Literal Interpretation. Follow instructions so poorly you cause damage. Destroy 'Bacon' or 'Gretel' cards.
cards.lore: "You should have cast friendly eyes on her... So he cut out all the calves' eyes and threw them in her face."
cards.gradeReason: "Destroy 'Bacon' or 'Gretel' cards" by literal misinterpretation is the Clever Hans card-type mechanic perfectly named — the lore proves the damage level achievable.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: horror folk art. Subject: boy holding a bag of eyeballs with an expression of complete sincerity. Mood: instructions followed.

cards.power: The Manager. Summons an 'Iron Army' or a 'Three-Legged Horse' depending on your need.
cards.lore: My power is great, greater than you think, and I have gold and silver in abundance.
cards.gradeReason: Both summoned entities — 'Iron Army' and 'Three-Legged Horse' — are undefined concepts; the power requires an infrastructure the deck never establishes.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: dark forest woodcut. Subject: rusted iron giant beckoning from a well, army and limping horse visible behind him. Mood: contingent threat.

cards.power: The Jobber Giant. High strength, low intelligence. Can be defeated by 'Bird' or 'Cheese.'
cards.lore: You are such a great fellow, and yet cannot even carry the tree!
cards.gradeReason: "Can be defeated by Bird or Cheese" is an outstanding type-weakness declaration — the most powerful unit in the deck is humbled by the most improbable counters.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: wrestling card. Subject: enormous figure holding a tree, looking confused at a very small cheese wheel. Mood: maximum strength, minimum coverage.

cards.power: Face Under the Mask. Defeat the 'Dwarf' to reveal true stats.
cards.lore: You would not feel me between your teeth... take these two wicked girls!
cards.gradeReason: Conditional reveal on Dwarf-defeat is a strong wrestling mechanic but depends on a Dwarf entity being in play — timing is everything and the table controls none of it.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: wrestling reveal engraving. Subject: bear mid-transformation into a prince, the disguise half-removed, two girls running. Mood: dramatic unmasking.

cards.power: The Curse. Put the entire 'Castle' faction to sleep for 100 turns.
cards.lore: She had not been asked to the feast... and set to work to take her revenge.
cards.gradeReason: Faction-wide sleep for 100 turns is the most dramatic faction nuke in the deck, but requires a Castle faction that is undefined in base Kayfabizarro.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: gothic ball engraving. Subject: fairy crashing a feast, every guest already mid-slump, spinning wheel visible in the corner. Mood: uninvited consequence.

cards.power: Donkey Transformation. Force opponent to eat. They lose all equipment and can only "Bray."
cards.lore: Scarcely were they swallowed when she lost her own form.
cards.gradeReason: Reducing a player to equipment-less braying is the most complete humiliation mechanic in the deck — the table will immediately try this on the most articulate player.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: dark kitchen engraving. Subject: plate of innocuous salad leaves with a donkey face reflected in the bowl. Mood: dietary consequence.

cards.power: Summon Stable. Summons the "Black Dwarf" to beat up judges and kings.
cards.lore: Strike down to earth that false judge there... and spare not the king.
cards.gradeReason: "Summons the Black Dwarf to beat up judges and kings" is seven words of pure anarchist clarity — the power knows exactly who its enemies are.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: smoky tavern woodcut. Subject: soldier lighting a pipe, small armored figure emerging from the smoke heading purposefully toward a courthouse. Mood: delegated justice.

cards.power: Pregnancy Cravings. Trade your "First Born" for this card.
cards.lore: She would have died if she had not got some to eat.
cards.gradeReason: Rapunzel's origin compressed to a vegetable transaction is conceptually precise but the power is a standard card-trade with an alarming cost label.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: gothic garden engraving. Subject: woman reaching through a wall for rapunzel leaves, a contract materializing in the moonlight. Mood: irresistible craving.

cards.power: Animal Talk. Understand the gossip of ducks and ants.
cards.lore: The king never took off the cover to eat of it until he was quite alone.
cards.gradeReason: "Understand the gossip of ducks and ants" is the most charming power description in the deck — the intelligence gathered is both real and absurd.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: naturalist woodcut. Subject: white snake coiled on a platter, surrounded by ducks and ants clearly mid-conversation. Mood: classified waterfowl.

cards.power: The Reveal. Remove cap to stun the audience. Win the "Golden Apple."
cards.lore: He took his pocket-handkerchief and tied it round his head, in order that the man might not see it.
cards.gradeReason: Physical cap removal as reveal-stunt is good wrestling theatre but "Win the Golden Apple" makes winning conditional on a token not defined in core play.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: disguise reveal woodcut. Subject: drab-capped figure in the act of removing the cap, golden light already escaping the edges. Mood: contained radiance.

cards.power: Wardrobe Change. Swap your "Rags" for "Ball Gown." Ignore "Step-Sisters."
cards.lore: Shake, shake, hazel-tree, Gold and silver over me!
cards.gradeReason: The "Ignore Step-Sisters" clause is the best mechanic on a clean but functional card — it names the threat and dismisses it in four words.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: folk woodcut. Subject: small tree dropping dresses onto a grave, a girl waiting below. Mood: maternal recursion.

cards.power: Hardcore Dedication. Cut off a body part to fit the "Gimmick Shoe."
cards.lore: Cut the heel off; when you are queen you will no longer have to go on foot.
cards.gradeReason: The extremity of dedication required to fit the Gimmick Shoe is the Cinderella story distilled to its most brutal logic — ambition as self-surgery.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: crime scene woodcut. Subject: ornate shoe next to a knife, blood spatter, no owner in frame. Mood: committed sacrifice.

cards.power: Busy Work. Opponent must roll 6s before they can go to the ball.
cards.lore: The good ones go into the pot, the bad ones go into your crop.
cards.gradeReason: Forcing an opponent to repeatedly attempt 6s as a gate is elegant cruelty — they will never feel as close to the ball as when they first roll a 5.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: domestic woodcut. Subject: pile of peas next to a fireplace, a scorecard showing no 6s yet, a ball visible in the distant window. Mood: patient obstruction.

cards.power: Quick Change. Transform into a "Lake" or "Flower" to avoid the "Witch."
cards.lore: "I counsel you first to take away her magic wand, or we cannot escape."
cards.gradeReason: Type-transformation for evasion is mechanically interesting but "Lake" and "Flower" as card types require a transformation system the deck doesn't define.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: folk horror woodcut. Subject: wand lying in a field, a lake and a flower visible where two figures had been, a witch approaching. Mood: last-second escape.

cards.power: Ventriloquism. Distract the pursuer. Delay turn by 3 rounds.
cards.lore: "Here, on the stairs, I am sweeping."
cards.gradeReason: Turn delay as distraction mechanic is clean and correct but it's the most standard interrupt in the deck — the ventriloquism framing is wasted on a plain timer.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: staircase horror woodcut. Subject: three blood drops on stairs, each with a speech bubble reading "Here, on the stairs, I am sweeping." Mood: automated alibi.

cards.power: The Bluff. Convince the "Murderers" you are learning cosmic secrets.
cards.lore: Compared to this seat, all the learning of the schools is as empty air.
cards.gradeReason: The concept is outstanding but "the Murderers" is an unexplained faction — without a defined threat the bluff has no target and no stakes.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: dark woodland engraving. Subject: man in a sack hanging from a tree, looking extremely studious, axe-wielders peering curiously. Mood: improvised authority.

cards.power: Divine Intervention. Receive exactly what you wish for.
cards.lore: You shall have a son with the power of wishing.
cards.gradeReason: "Receive exactly what you wish for" is undefined — no mechanism, no cost, no constraint — the card grants everything and specifies nothing.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: sacred object woodcut. Subject: ornate ring on a stone altar, a wish-form in the air above it dissolving without fulfillment. Mood: unlimited inaccessibility.

cards.power: The Rope Break. Climb out of reach. If cut, you take fall damage.
cards.lore: "Rapunzel, Rapunzel, Let down your hair to me."
cards.gradeReason: Reach mechanic with a danger-if-severed condition is elegant but "fall damage" needs a mechanic definition — it implies HP rules that don't exist.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: tower woodcut. Subject: impossibly long braid hanging from a high tower, a figure halfway up, scissors visible below. Mood: structural vulnerability.

cards.power: Promotional Greed. Demand a Title Shot, then the Company, then Godhood. Return to 'Pigsty' on fail.
cards.lore: "My wife Ilsabill, Will have her own will."
cards.gradeReason: Escalating promotion demands with a catastrophic reset to Pigsty is the most sustained narrative arc compressed into a single power — three wishes and a punishment in one sentence.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: wrestling championship hierarchy poster. Subject: woman on a throne, then a larger throne, then clouds, then a pigsty, all connected by arrows. Mood: inevitable regression.

cards.power: The Time Limit Draw. The match stops for 100 years. Everyone sleeps.
cards.lore: "The thorns and bushes laid hold of them... and there they stuck fast, and died wretchedly."
cards.gradeReason: Making the entire table go dormant is the most physically committed pause mechanic in the corpus — "for 100 years" is a duration no one will agree to and that disagreement IS the card.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: gothic garden engraving. Subject: entire gaming table frozen mid-game, thorns growing slowly over the cards, a 100-year scoreboard in the corner. Mood: enforced patience.

cards.power: The Masked Wrestler. Conceal identity. Cook soup. Reveal 'Golden Dress' later.
cards.lore: "I am good for nothing but to be scullion-girl, and to have boots and shoes thrown at my head."
cards.gradeReason: Three-phase strategy in a power is inventive but phase two ("Cook soup") has no mechanic and phase three requires a Golden Dress card to pay off.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: wrestling reveal illustration. Subject: scullery girl in fur coat at a stove, golden dress visible folded in the pocket. Mood: long game.

verdict: Grimm Set 02 pulls off the rare double-kayfabe — wrestling rules mapped onto fairy tale logic mapped onto childhood trauma, three layers deep. Named strength: Clever Elsie, Sleeping Beauty, The Fisherman's Wife, and The Peas in Ashes are four consecutive knockout design moments that no other deck in this corpus matches for sustained dark comedy mechanics. Named weakness: roughly a third of powers reference undefined card types — Stepmother, Dog faction, False Bride, Haunted Tower — requiring a pre-game glossary session most pickup tables won't run. The pre-printed R/A/F stat blocks add TCG dimension the core dice-slot format doesn't support, making cross-deck play complicated until someone publishes a conversion ruling. Table-ready: Yes, with a five-minute setup conversation about faction types.
blurb: Fairy tales as pro wrestling moves — 52 cards that transform Grimm characters into kayfabe archetypes. For game masters, drama teachers, and anyone who ever suspected Sleeping Beauty was a worked finish.

coverQA.coverVisual: 4 — wrestling-meets-Grimm imagery follows the strong Kayfabizarro card template; cover likely depicts fairy tale silhouettes with ring ropes or championship belt motifs
coverQA.coverTitle: 5 — 'The Fairy Tale Screwjob' is a perfect title; announces the mashup and the irreverence in six words
coverQA.coverVibeMatch: 5 — title telegraphs exactly what is inside: fairy tale content submitted to wrestling kayfabe treatment
coverQA.coverOriginality: 4 — expansion set concept is proven from Set 01 but the Screwjob subtitle adds fresh anarchist framing
coverQA.coverViral: 4 — 'Fairy Tale Screwjob' is genuinely quotable; strong Instagram caption potential
coverQA.coverNote: The subtitle does all the heavy lifting: 'The Fairy Tale Screwjob' lands in one swing. Cover scores high on concept-telegraphing and title virality; slight dock for being an expansion set, which primes buyers for 'second album' energy rather than first-impression impact. Still the best subtitle in the Grimm sub-corpus.

notes:
**Pre-printed R/A/F stats — fundamental format difference:** Unlike all previously analyzed decks, this expansion uses pre-printed numerical R/A/F values (0–6) on every card. These are stat blocks, not blank dice slots. RAF = true, but the R/A/F system is functioning as a TCG power-rating system (Resonance/Amplitude/Frequency as pre-set numbers) rather than dice-roll prompts. This creates a hybrid between the Kayfabizarro storytelling format and a conventional TCG. Cross-deck play with dice-slot format cards will require a conversion ruling.

**Grimm Gimmicks numbering gap:** Section headers visible on card pages: GRIMM GIMMICKS (unnumbered, page 3), GRIMM GIMMICKS II (page 5), GRIMM GIMMICKS III (page 6), GRIMM GIMMICKS IV (page 8), GRIMM GIMMICKS VI (page 10), GRIMM GIMMICKS VIII (page 12). Sections V and VII are not labeled (pages 9 and 11 carry no section header). Either two sections were intentionally left unlabeled or section numbering is non-consecutive by design. Parser note: card numbering in this analysis runs sequentially 01–52 regardless of section labeling.

**Repeat entities vs. Grimm deck 01:** Multiple entities from the previous Grimm deck (Kayfab-Fairy Tales) reappear here with different powers and stat blocks: The Golden Goose, The Turnip, Straw Coal & Bean, Rumpelstiltskin, Iron Hans, The Giant, The Blue Light, The White Snake, The Fisherman's Wife, Cat-Skin. These are intentional reimaginings, not errors — the wrestling format produces distinct translations of the same source character. Both versions should be retained as corpus entries; the comparison is editorially useful.

**Verbatim Grimm lore:** Unlike the invented satirical lore in Grimm deck 01, this deck quotes the original Grimm texts directly in lore fields. Copyright status of 19th-century Brothers Grimm translations: public domain. No IP concern.

**Page 2 is a setup/instructions page** ("CUT & BLEED INSTRUCTIONS"), not a card page. Card pages begin on page 3.

**Page 16 is a Kayfabe Currency tokens page** (Golden Apple, Pea, Pearl, Breadcrumb, Drop of Blood, FrizzleBob Coin marked "NO VALUE"). Not cards. Introduces a token economy not present in the previous Grimm deck — the currency types (Golden Apple, Pea, Pearl) presumably correspond to card powers referencing these tokens, establishing a cross-deck economy.

urgent: Faction system: approximately 18 of 52 cards reference undefined card types ('Child,' 'Stepmother,' 'Dog faction,' 'Castle faction,' 'False Bride,' 'Horse,' 'Dwarf,' 'Murderers,' 'Golden Cage,' 'Haunted Tower,' 'Mountain,' 'Castle'). Either publish a faction glossary as a companion page or convert the affected powers to faction-free language. Without this, the freestyleCompatibility score cannot rise above 5.

THE BARREL OF NAILS (card 28): "The Final Bump. The ultimate punishment for a 'False Bride.'" defines no action. Replace with a specific mechanic — e.g., "Discard the False Bride card permanently. All 'False Bride' effects are reversed."
THE WISHING RING (card 48): "Receive exactly what you wish for" is undefined. Add a cost and a constraint — the tale requires both.
quickWins: THE WATER OF LIFE (card 22): "Beware of switching fluids" is editorial, not mechanical. Add: "If a 'Brother' card is in play, they may substitute a 'Sea-Water' card instead."
THE WISHING CLOAK (card 23): Location travel requires no board in Kayfabizarro. Convert to: "Teleport: Skip past the current Quest constraint. Go directly to the next phase."
THE POISON COMB (card 07): "Until the lace is cut or comb removed" needs table-executable conditions — e.g., "Until another player plays a 'Scissors' or 'Hunter' card, or the opponent rolls a 6."
niceToHave: THE GOLDEN GOOSE (card 01): "Cannot tag out" needs translation for non-wrestling tables — e.g., "Opponent cannot discard this card or pass it this turn."

THE LUMP OF SILVER (card 02): The trade chain (Horse → Cow → Pig → Stone) needs named placeholder cards or a clear rule about what "Horse" means at tables without those cards. Consider printing a reference track on the card itself.

Grimm Gimmicks numbering: labeled sections jump I → II → III → IV → VI → VIII, skipping V and VII. Whether deliberate or editorial oversight, it needs a decision — if intentional, a footnote would prevent parser confusion.

marketingText:
Kayfabizarro: GRIMMS' KAYFABE LEGENDS – The Fairy Tale Screwjob (Free Cut & Play Comic Card Game)

In wrestling, a screwjob is a finish the audience never agreed to. The fairy tale was the first one.

Watch what these cards do at a table. Sleeping Beauty stops the whole match for a hundred years and dares anyone to actually agree to the pause. Clever Elsie makes every player weep over a disaster that has not happened and never will, and somebody always refuses, which starts a second fight on top of the first. The Fisherman's Wife demands a title shot, then the whole company, then godhood, and crashes straight back to the pigsty on a failed roll. The Severed Heel cuts off a body part to fit the gimmick shoe, because ambition was always self-surgery and the original said so in plain language. None of this is the softened bedtime cut. This is the Brothers Grimm at full contact, the second pass through the canon, with the lore quoted verbatim so the source can defend itself.

This is Social Story Wrestling where the rigged ending is the whole sport. You pick up a card, perform the wholesome read with a straight face, and the table rules whether it survives the worked finish underneath. Fifty-two archetypes, each one a move you commit to out loud, each one carrying its own printed risk.

WHAT'S INSIDE?
- The Screwjob Core Deck: 52 High-Res "Print, Cut & Play" Cards, the second turn through the Grimm canon, featuring Clever Elsie, Rumpelstiltskin, and The Fisherman's Wife, every power quoting the tale it was born from.
- The Freestyle Rules: the complete Anti-Rulebook. No complicated math, just storytelling, dice-driven chaos, and the part where every card can claim anything until the room calls the bluff. This set prints R/A/F stats straight onto the card, so the bragging is on the table before you even play it.
- The Kayfabe Currency: a token economy of Golden Apples, Peas, Pearls, Breadcrumbs and Drops of Blood, plus a FrizzleBob Coin stamped NO VALUE, because the most honest currency in the canon is the one that admits it has none.

WHY "PAY WHAT YOU WANT"?
I make these because the public domain is the one inheritance nobody can repossess, and the Grimms have been sanded smooth for two centuries while their teeth were still good. Broke? Enter "0" and take it. Cut it out, play it, put the archetype in a headlock. Want to support the craft? Every dollar goes straight into the next stack of cards. Share freely, attribute honestly, never resell. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

Choose your reality. Become an Epistemic Outlaw.
"Every happy ending is a finish somebody booked. Read the booking, then write your own."
Stay fluffy. — Uncle FrizzleBob
